text:
Match List - I with List - II.

  

    List - I
Mass of substance

    List - II
Number of atoms

  

  

    A.

    1.8 mg water

    I.

    $2\times 10^{-4}\times \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$

  

  

    B.

    9.8 mg sulphuric acid

    II.

    $1.5\times 10^{-4}\times \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$

  

  

    C.

    1.8 mg carbon

    III.

    $3\times 10^{-4}\times \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$

  

  

    D.

    5.85 mg salt $(\mathrm{NaCl})$

    IV.

    $7\times 10^{-4}\times \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$

  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the total number of atoms in each given mass, we use the relation:

$\text{Number of moles}=\frac{\text{Given mass in grams}}{\text{Molar mass in g/mol}}$

$\text{Total number of atoms}=\text{Moles}\times N_{A}\times \text{Number of atoms in one formula unit/molecule}$

A. $1.8\text{mg}$ of water ($\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$):

Molar mass of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}=18\text{g/mol}$

Mass $=1.8\text{mg}=1.8\times 10^{-3}\text{g}$

$\text{Moles of}\text{H}_{2}\text{O}=\frac{1.8\times 10^{-3}}{18}=10^{-4}\text{mol}$

Since $1$ molecule of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ contains $3$ atoms ($2\text{H}+1\text{O}$):

$\text{Number of atoms}=3\times 10^{-4}\times N_{A}$

This matches with III.

B. $9.8\text{mg}$ of sulphuric acid ($\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$):

Molar mass of $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}=98\text{g/mol}$

Mass $=9.8\text{mg}=9.8\times 10^{-3}\text{g}$

$\text{Moles of}\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}=\frac{9.8\times 10^{-3}}{98}=10^{-4}\text{mol}$

Since $1$ molecule of $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ contains $7$ atoms ($2\text{H}+1\text{S}+4\text{O}$):

$\text{Number of atoms}=7\times 10^{-4}\times N_{A}$

This matches with IV.

C. $1.8\text{mg}$ of carbon ($\text{C}$):

Molar mass of $\text{C}=12\text{g/mol}$

Mass $=1.8\text{mg}=1.8\times 10^{-3}\text{g}$

$\text{Moles of}\text{C}=\frac{1.8\times 10^{-3}}{12}=1.5\times 10^{-4}\text{mol}$

Since carbon is atomic (1 atom per unit):

$\text{Number of atoms}=1.5\times 10^{-4}\times N_{A}$

This matches with II.

D. $5.85\text{mg}$ of salt ($\text{NaCl}$):

Molar mass of $\text{NaCl}=58.5\text{g/mol}$

Mass $=5.85\text{mg}=5.85\times 10^{-3}\text{g}$

$\text{Moles of}\text{NaCl}=\frac{5.85\times 10^{-3}}{58.5}=10^{-4}\text{mol}$

Since $1$ formula unit of $\text{NaCl}$ contains $2$ atoms ($1\text{Na}+1\text{Cl}$):

$\text{Number of atoms}=2\times 10^{-4}\times N_{A}$

This matches with I.

Combining these results:

A $\to$ III

B $\to$ IV

C $\to$ II

D $\to$ I

The correct choice is Option C.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Given below are two statements :

Given : Molar mass of $\mathrm{C},\mathrm{H},\mathrm{O},\mathrm{Cl}$ are $12,1,16$ and $35.5\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$, respectively

Statement I : In $30%(\mathrm{w}/\mathrm{w})$ solution of methanol in $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}($ at T K$)$, the mole fraction of $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}$ is equal to 0.33 .

Statement II : Mixture of methanol and $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}$ shows positive deviation from Raoult's law. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In 100 g of the 30 % (w/w) mixture, methanol $=30\text{g}$ and $\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}=70\text{g}$.

Molar masses: $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{OH}=12+4(1)+16=32\text{g mol}^{-1}$ and $\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}=12+4(35.5)=154\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

$n_{\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{OH}}=\dfrac{30}{32}=0.9375\text{mol},n_{\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}}=\dfrac{70}{154}=0.4545\text{mol}$

$x_{\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}}=\dfrac{0.4545}{0.9375+0.4545}=\dfrac{0.4545}{1.392}=0.33$

So Statement I is true.

Methanol molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds. Non-polar $\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}$ molecules come in between them and break some of these hydrogen bonds, while the methanol–$\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}$ attractions that replace them are much weaker. The molecules escape more easily, so the vapour pressure is higher than Raoult's law predicts: a positive deviation. So Statement II is true.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: Bromine trifluoride autoionizes to form $\mathrm{BrF}_{2}^{⊕}$ and $\mathrm{BrF}_{4}^{⊖}$. The shapes of the cation and anion are respectively $____$ and $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
First, let us recall the autoionization of bromine trifluoride:

$2~\mathrm{BrF}_{3}⇌\mathrm{BrF}_{2}^{+}+\mathrm{BrF}_{4}^{-}$

We have to determine the shapes of the cation and the anion.

Central atom: Br  

Valence electrons of Br = 7  

Each F contributes one bond → 2 Br–F bonds = 2 pairs of bonding electrons

So, total electrons around Br for shape determination:

$7-2(\text{by bonding})-1(\text{positive charge})=4$

These 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs on Br.

Hence, the total number of electron pairs around Br =  

2 (bonding) + 2 (lone pairs) = 4 electron domains.

According to VSEPR theory:  

4 electron pairs → tetrahedral electron geometry  

With 2 bonding and 2 lone pairs → bent shape

Thus, $\mathrm{BrF}_{2}^{+}$ is bent.

Central atom: Br  

Valence electrons of Br = 7  

Each F contributes one bond → 4 Br–F bonds = 4 pairs of bonding electrons  

Additional one electron due to negative charge → +1

Hence total electrons on central bromine:

$7+1-4=4$

which means 2 lone pairs on Br.

Thus, the total number of electron pairs =  

4 (bonding) + 2 (lone pairs) = 6 electron domains.

According to VSEPR theory:  

6 electron domains → octahedral electron geometry  

With 4 bonding and 2 lone pairs → square planar shape

Shapes are:

$\mathrm{BrF}_{2}^{+}$ → bent

$\mathrm{BrF}_{4}^{-}$ → square planar

Correct Option: A) bent, square planar
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Which of the following statements are not correct?

A. For water, magnitude of $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}$ is more than the magnitude of $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}$.

B. The elevation in boiling point of water when a non-volatile solute is added to it is larger in magnitude than its depression in freezing point.

C. Osmotic pressure measurement is preferred over any other colligative property to determine molar mass of proteins and polymers.

D. The dimerised form of benzoic acid in benzene is 
[IMG]


Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For water, $K_{b}=0.52\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ and $K_{f}=1.86\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$, so $K_{b}<K_{f}$ and statement A is incorrect.

For the same molality $m$, $\Delta T_{b}=K_{b}m$ and $\Delta T_{f}=K_{f}m$, so the elevation in boiling point is smaller than the depression in freezing point and statement B is incorrect.

Osmotic pressure is measured at room temperature and is large enough to measure even at the very low molar concentrations of proteins and polymers, so it is the preferred method and statement C is correct.

In benzene, benzoic acid forms a cyclic dimer held by two $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\cdots \mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}$ hydrogen bonds, each OH bonded to the C=O of the other molecule; the structure shown has only one hydrogen bond, so statement D is incorrect.

The incorrect statements are A, B and D.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

solution.body:
Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely held (outermost) electron from a neutral atom.

Ionization energy generally increases when the effective nuclear charge increases. This happens because the nucleus attracts the valence electron more strongly, so more energy is required to remove it.

Also, some electronic configurations are extra stable. Electrons in stable configurations are harder to remove, so their ionization energy is higher.

Fully filled orbitals have greater ionisation energy due to stable electronic configuration.

Order of I.E:
$\text{fully-filled orbital}>\text{Half-filled orbital}>\text{Partially filled orbital}$

Here $n=2$, so we are comparing configurations of elements in the 2nd period. As we move from $s$-block to $p$-block in the same period, atomic size decreases and effective nuclear charge increases, so ionisation energy generally increases.

Using stability ideas: the configuration $ns^{2}np^{6}$ (noble gas, fully filled) has the maximum ionisation energy, and $ns^{2}np^{1}$ has comparatively lower ionisation energy.

So the decreasing order is: $D>C>A>B$

text:
Find the correct statements related to group 15 hydrides.

A. Reducing nature increases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

B. Tendency to donate lone pair of electrons decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

C. The stability of hydrides decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

D. HEH bond angle decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{SbH}_{3}(\mathrm{E}=$ Elements of group 15)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For group 15 hydrides, the hydrides are:

$\mathrm{NH}_{3},\mathrm{PH}_{3},\mathrm{AsH}_{3},\mathrm{SbH}_{3},\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

Now let us check each statement one by one.

A. Reducing nature increases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$
Down the group, the $E-H$ bond strength decreases because the size of the central atom increases.

So, the hydrides can release hydrogen more easily and hence their reducing character increases down the group.

Thus,

$\mathrm{NH}_{3}<\mathrm{PH}_{3}<\mathrm{AsH}_{3}<\mathrm{SbH}_{3}<\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

in reducing nature.

So, A is correct.

B. Tendency to donate lone pair of electrons decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$
All group 15 hydrides have one lone pair on the central atom.  

But down the group, the atomic size increases and the lone pair becomes more diffuse and less available for donation.

Hence, basic character decreases down the group:

$\mathrm{NH}_{3}>\mathrm{PH}_{3}>\mathrm{AsH}_{3}>\mathrm{SbH}_{3}>\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

So, the tendency to donate lone pair decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$.

Therefore, B is correct.

C. The stability of hydrides decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$
As we move down the group, the size of the central atom increases and the overlap between $E$ and $H$ orbitals becomes poorer.

Therefore, the $E-H$ bond becomes weaker and thermal stability decreases.

So,

$\mathrm{NH}_{3}>\mathrm{PH}_{3}>\mathrm{AsH}_{3}>\mathrm{SbH}_{3}>\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$

in stability.

Hence, C is correct.

D. $H-E-H$ bond angle decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{SbH}_{3}$
The bond angles are approximately:

$\mathrm{NH}_{3}\approx 107.5^{\circ }$

$\mathrm{PH}_{3}\approx 93.5^{\circ }$

$\mathrm{AsH}_{3}\approx 92^{\circ }$

$\mathrm{SbH}_{3}\approx 91^{\circ }$

So, the bond angle indeed decreases from $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to $\mathrm{SbH}_{3}$.

Therefore, D is correct.

Since all four statements are correct, the correct option is:

$\text{Option C: A, B, C and D}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Given below are two statements for catalytic properties of transition metals.

Statement I : First row transition metals which act as catalyst utilise their 3d electrons only for formation of bonds between reactant molecules and atoms on the surface of catalyst.

Statement II : There is increase in the concentration of reactants on the surface of catalyst which strengthens the bonds in reacting molecules.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The first-row transition metals use both their 3d and 4s electrons to form bonds with reactant molecules on the surface of the catalyst.

∴ Statement I is incorrect.

When reactants are adsorbed on the catalytic surface, their concentration on the surface increases, but this adsorption actually weakens the bonds within the reactant molecules. This helps in forming an activated complex and reduces the activation energy of the reaction.

∴ Statement II is incorrect.

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : Vapours of the liquid with higher boiling point condense before vapours of the liquid with lower boiling points in fractional distillation.

Statement II : The vapours rising up in the fractionating column become richer in high boiling component of the mixture.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let us analyse both statements carefully using the concept of fractional distillation as given in NCERT.

Concept:  

Fractional distillation is a process used to separate a mixture of two or more liquids having different boiling points.  

The liquid having a lower boiling point vaporises first.  

As vapours rise through the fractionating column, they repeatedly condense and vaporise.  

The temperature in the column gradually decreases from bottom to top.  

Hence, vapours rising upwards become richer in the more volatile (lower boiling point) component.

Statement I
“Vapours of the liquid with higher boiling point condense before vapours of the liquid with lower boiling points in fractional distillation.”

Liquids with higher boiling point are less volatile.  

Thus, their vapours condense earlier (lower in the column) because they require a lower temperature difference to liquefy.  

Therefore, Statement I is true.

Statement II
“The vapours rising up in the fractionating column become richer in high boiling component of the mixture.”

As explained, the rising vapours become richer in the low boiling or more volatile component, not the high boiling one.  

Therefore, Statement II is false.

Correct Answer:
Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: $\text{The major product of which of the following reaction is not obtained by rearrangement reaction?}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
(A) $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}$ with anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl}{}_{3}$ gives a primary propyl cation, which undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable isopropyl cation; benzene is then alkylated to isopropylbenzene (cumene). The product comes from rearrangement.

(B) tert-Butyl alcohol, $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{3}\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{OH}$, is protonated and loses water to give the tertiary tert-butyl cation directly; loss of $\mathrm{H}{}^{+}$ gives 2-methylpropene, $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{2}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$. A tertiary cation has no more stable cation to shift to, so no rearrangement occurs.

(C) n-Hexane with anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl}{}_{3}$/HCl isomerises to 2-methylpentane: the carbocation formed on the chain rearranges (hydride and alkyl shifts) to a branched tertiary cation, so the carbon skeleton itself changes.

(D) Neopentyl alcohol, $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{3}\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$, would give a primary neopentyl cation; a 1,2-methyl shift converts it into the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation, which loses $\mathrm{H}{}^{+}$ to give 2-methylbut-2-ene, $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{2}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$. The product comes from rearrangement.

Only in (B) is the major product formed without rearrangement.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
The total number of aromatic compounds/species from the following is

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A species is aromatic when it has a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with $(4n+2)$ $π$ electrons (Hückel rule); a compound containing such a ring is an aromatic compound.

p-Benzoquinone: the two $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ $π$ bonds are outside the ring, so the ring is cross-conjugated and has no continuous cycle of $(4n+2)$ $π$ electrons: non-aromatic.

Tropylium ion, $\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{7}{}^{+}$: seven $sp^{2}$ carbons in a planar ring with 6 $π$ electrons ($n=1$): aromatic.

Phenanthrene: planar, fully conjugated tricyclic system with 14 $π$ electrons ($n=3$): aromatic.

1,2-Dihydronaphthalene: the $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$ unit interrupts conjugation only in one ring; the other ring is an intact benzene ring with 6 $π$ electrons, so the compound is aromatic.

Cyclobutadiene dication, $\mathrm{C}{}_{4}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}{}^{2+}$: four $sp^{2}$ carbons in a planar ring with 2 $π$ electrons ($n=0$): aromatic.

Cyclohexadienyl anion, $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{7}{}^{-}$: the $sp^{3}$ $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$ carbon breaks the cyclic conjugation: non-aromatic.

Aromatic species: tropylium ion, phenanthrene, 1,2-dihydronaphthalene and cyclobutadiene dication, a total of 4.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

Hot aqueous NaOH then hydrolyses the lactam: the ring C(=O)–N bond breaks, opening the ring to a carboxylate and a secondary amine.

Acidification converts $\mathrm{COO}{}^{-}$ to COOH, so P is $\mathrm{HOOC}-(\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}){}_{4}-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3})-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$.

Option (D), with $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ in place of COOH, would need reduction of the amide carbonyl, which $\mathrm{NaBH}{}_{4}$ does not bring about.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: The incorrect statement from the following with respect to carbohydrates is :
options: The monosaccharide units obtained from hydrolysis of oligosaccharides are always the same.
Starch and cellulose are typical examples of polysaccharides, which are very high molecular weight compounds of more than ten monosaccharide units.
Open chain and cyclic structures co-exist at equilibrium that are responsible for certain properties as in the case of $\mathrm{D}-(+)$-glucose.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
(A) Every monosaccharide has a free aldehyde group or an $α$-hydroxy ketone group, so all monosaccharides reduce Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution; the statement is correct.

(B) The units obtained from an oligosaccharide may or may not be the same: maltose gives two glucose units, but sucrose gives glucose and fructose and lactose gives glucose and galactose. The statement "always the same" is incorrect.

$\text{Lactose}\leftarrow ^{\mathrm{H}{}_{3}\mathrm{O}{}^{+}}\text{Glucose}+\text{Galactose},\text{Maltose}\leftarrow ^{\mathrm{H}{}_{3}\mathrm{O}{}^{+}}\text{Glucose}+\text{Glucose}$

(C) Starch and cellulose are polysaccharides made of a very large number (far more than ten) of glucose units and have very high molar masses; the statement is correct.

(D) D-(+)-Glucose exists as an equilibrium mixture of the open-chain form and the cyclic $α$ and $β$ forms, which accounts for properties such as mutarotation; the statement is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Number of paramagnetic complexes among the following is $____$ .

$\begin{array}{l} [\mathrm{MnBr}_{4}]^{2-},[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}]^{2-},[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}]^{2-},[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_{4}],[\mathrm{CoF}_{6}]^{3-},[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]^{4-},[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]^{3-},[\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]^{3-}, \\ [\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+},[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4})_{3}]^{3-} \end{array}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A complex is paramagnetic when it has at least one unpaired electron ($n>0$); $n$ follows from the oxidation state of the metal, the geometry and the ligand field strength.

$[\mathrm{MnBr}{}_{4}]{}^{2-}$: $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{2+}$, $3d^{5}$, tetrahedral with weak-field $\mathrm{Br}{}^{-}$, $e^{2}t_{2}^{3}$, so $n=5$ (paramagnetic).

$[\mathrm{NiCl}{}_{4}]{}^{2-}$: $\mathrm{Ni}{}^{2+}$, $3d^{8}$, tetrahedral ($sp^{3}$) with weak-field $\mathrm{Cl}{}^{-}$, $e^{4}t_{2}^{4}$, so $n=2$ (paramagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{4}]{}^{2-}$: $\mathrm{Ni}{}^{2+}$, $3d^{8}$; strong-field $\mathrm{CN}{}^{-}$ pairs the electrons and the complex is square planar ($dsp^{2}$), so $n=0$ (diamagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO}){}_{4}]$: $\mathrm{Ni}$ in the zero oxidation state, $3d^{8}4s^{2}$; strong-field $\mathrm{CO}$ pairs the $4s$ electrons into $3d$, giving $3d^{10}$ and tetrahedral $sp^{3}$ bonding, so $n=0$ (diamagnetic).

$[\mathrm{CoF}{}_{6}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$, $3d^{6}$, weak-field $\mathrm{F}{}^{-}$, high spin $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$, so $n=4$ (paramagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{4-}$: $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{2+}$, $3d^{6}$, strong-field $\mathrm{CN}{}^{-}$, low spin $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$, so $n=0$ (diamagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{3+}$, $3d^{4}$, low spin $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{0}$; four electrons in three $t_{2g}$ orbitals leave two of them singly occupied, so $n=2$ (paramagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Ti}{}^{3+}$, $3d^{1}$, $t_{2g}^{1}e_{g}^{0}$, so $n=1$ (paramagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{6}]{}^{2+}$: $\mathrm{Cu}{}^{2+}$, $3d^{9}$, $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{3}$, so $n=1$ (paramagnetic).

$[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}){}_{3}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$, $3d^{6}$; the high charge on $\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$ makes $\Delta _{o}$ larger than the pairing energy even with oxalate, so the complex is low spin $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ ($d^{2}sp^{3}$) and $n=0$ (diamagnetic).

The paramagnetic complexes are $[\mathrm{MnBr}{}_{4}]{}^{2-}$, $[\mathrm{NiCl}{}_{4}]{}^{2-}$, $[\mathrm{CoF}{}_{6}]{}^{3-}$, $[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{3-}$, $[\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{3-}$ and $[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{6}]{}^{2+}$.

Hence, the answer is 6.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Consider two radiations of wavelengths

$λ_{1}=2000\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{o}}$

$λ_{2}=6000\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{o}}$

The ratio of the energies of these two radiations $\left (\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}\right )$ is $____$ (Nearest integer).
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We know that the energy of a photon is given by the formula  

$E=\frac{hc}{λ}$

where  

$h$ = Planck’s constant  

$c$ = velocity of light  

$λ$ = wavelength of the radiation.

For the two radiations,

$\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}=\frac{\frac{hc}{λ1}}{\frac{hc}{λ2}}=\frac{λ_{2}}{λ_{1}}$

$λ_{1}=2000\text{Å},λ_{2}=6000\text{Å}$

$\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}=\frac{6000}{2000}$

$\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}=3$

Final Answer
$\dfrac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}=3$

Hence, the ratio of energies of the two radiations is 3 (nearest integer).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Consider the reaction

$2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{g})+3\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\to 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})+2\mathrm{SO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$

The magnitude of enthalpy change for the reaction in $\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ is $____$ . (Nearest integer)

$\begin{array}{ll} Given: & \Delta _{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{H}^{⊖}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S})=-20.1\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ \Delta _{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{H}^{⊖}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})=-286.0\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ \Delta _{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{H}^{⊖}(\mathrm{SO}_{2})=-297.0\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \end{array}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We are given the reaction:  

$2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}(g)+3\mathrm{O}_{2}(g)\to 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(l)+2\mathrm{SO}_{2}(g)$

We are also given the standard enthalpies of formation:

$\begin{array}{ll} \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}) & =-20.1\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}) & =-286.0\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\mathrm{SO}_{2}) & =-297.0\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \end{array}$

According to NCERT convention,

$\Delta _{r}H^{\circ }=\sum \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\text{products})-\sum \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\text{reactants})$

Products:

$2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(l)+2\mathrm{SO}_{2}(g)$

$\sum \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\text{products})=[2(-286.0)+2(-297.0)]\mathrm{kJ}$

$=(-572.0-594.0)=-1166.0\mathrm{kJ}$

Reactants:

$2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}(g)+3\mathrm{O}_{2}(g)$

$\sum \Delta _{f}H^{\circ }(\text{reactants})=[2(-20.1)+3(0)]\mathrm{kJ}=-40.2\mathrm{kJ}$

$\Delta _{r}H^{\circ }=(-1166.0)-(-40.2)=-1125.8\mathrm{kJ}$

The magnitude of enthalpy change is

$|\Delta _{r}H^{\circ }|=1126\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}(\text{nearest integer})$

Final Answer
$1126\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Solid carbon, CaO and $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ are mixed and allowed to attain equilibrium at T K .

$\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{CaCO}_{3}(\mathrm{s})⇌\mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) & \mathrm{Kp}_{1}=0.08\mathrm{atm} \\ \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌2\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) & \mathrm{Kp}_{2}=2\mathrm{atm} \end{array}$

The partial pressure of CO is $__$ $\times 10^{-1}\mathrm{atm}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
First, let's consider the first equilibrium:

$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}(\mathrm{s})⇌\mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})K_{p_{1}}=0.08\mathrm{atm}$

As we know from our study of chemical equilibrium, for the equilibrium constant expression $K_{p}$, we only consider the partial pressures of the gaseous species. The concentrations of pure solids (like $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{CaO}$) are considered to be unity (1).

So, for this reaction, the expression for $K_{p_{1}}$ is:

$K_{p_{1}}=p_{CO_{2}}$

We are given that $K_{p_{1}}=0.08\mathrm{atm}$.

Therefore, the partial pressure of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ at equilibrium is fixed by this reaction.

$p_{CO_{2}}=0.08\mathrm{atm}$

This is an important first step. The presence of both $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}(\mathrm{s})$ and $\mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s})$ ensures that the partial pressure of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ is maintained at this value.

Now, let's look at the second equilibrium:

$\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌2\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g})K_{p_{2}}=2\mathrm{atm}$

Again, we write the expression for $K_{p_{2}}$. We consider the solid carbon, $\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s})$, to have an activity of 1.

$K_{p_{2}}=\frac{(p_{CO})^{2}}{p_{CO2}}$

Since both reactions are taking place in the same vessel and are at equilibrium, the partial pressure of the common species, $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$, must be the same for both.

We have already found that $p_{CO_{2}}=0.08\mathrm{atm}$ from the first equilibrium. We also know that $K_{p_{2}}=2\mathrm{atm}$. Let's substitute these values into the expression for $K_{p_{2}}$:

$2=\frac{(p_{CO})^{2}}{0.08}$

$\Rightarrow$ $(p_{CO})^{2}=2\times 0.08$

$\Rightarrow$ $(p_{CO})^{2}=0.16$

$\Rightarrow$ $p_{CO}=\sqrt{0.16}$

$\Rightarrowp_{CO}=0.4\mathrm{atm}$

$\Rightarrow$ $p_{CO}=4\times 10^{-1}\mathrm{atm}$.

Therefore, the value to be filled in the blank is 4.
